title: Nowruz, the new day
hookLine: the Persian new year at the spring equinox, kept across faiths and nations; Ferdowsi's Jamshid on his shining throne, and two ways of keeping the day
tomorrow: a boy sat in a fire on his aunt's lap. who walked out?

lines: THEY CALL IT THE NEW DAY.
cards: Somewhere this spring, a family will set a table with sprouting green shoots, apples, coins and a mirror, and wait for the minute of the equinox. That's Nowruz.

The Persian Book of Kings, Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, tells how the day got its name. King Jamshid has a throne made, set with jewels, and the demons lift it into the air. He sits in it, shining like the sun in the sky.
The world gathers in wonder and scatters jewels before him. And they call that day the new day.

teach.b: Nowruz means just that: new day. It begins at the spring equinox, when light and dark stand even, and families of more than one faith and nation keep it. So is it a holy day, or a family new year?
Ask around, and you'll hear both from people who love it.
For Zoroastrians, followers of the old Persian faith, Nowruz is a holy festival, creation made new, kept with prayers and a bright fire. The Baha'i faith keeps Naw-Ruz as a holy day too.

For some Muslim families in Iran and beyond, and for secular ones, it is first a family new year: a cleaned house, visits to elders, a table. One side says: take the faith out, and you lose what the day is for.
The other says: Nowruz belongs to everyone who keeps it, and that's why it has lasted. Under both is a teaching Ferdowsi's story carries.
The Shahnameh goes on: Jamshid grew proud and said he alone had made the world, and the divine glory left him.
The new day was never his to keep. Some readers see the same lesson on the haft-sin table, in the sabzeh, green sprouts someone grew patiently over days: new life, received and grown, not grabbed.

how: Families keeping Nowruz clean the house, set a haft-sin table with sprouted greens (sabzeh), apples, coins, a mirror and other items, gather at the moment of the spring equinox, and visit elders in the days after. Zoroastrians and Baha'is keep it as a holy day.

games.q: at a Nowruz table, a Muslim host says it's a family new year; her Zoroastrian friend calls it a holy festival. what's fair to say?
o: both hold real views: holy for some, a family new year for others.
the friend is right, so Muslims shouldn't keep Nowruz at all.
it's only a party; no faith has anything to do with it.
games.why: Nowruz is a holy day for Zoroastrians and Baha'is and a family new year for other households. both views come from people who keep it.

practice: If there's anything green near you, a plant, an herb, a leaf from outside, set it in front of you. Look at it closely for a minute: the new edge, the color.
When spring comes, you could set a small table with it, and one thing more, for a new day.
